title: Response to Migan (Team3DAlpha) - PROGRESSIVE OVERLOAD IS NOT THE DRIVER OF MUSC
summary: Point-by-point response to Team3DAlpha's video arguing progressive overload is not the main driver of hypertrophy. NH agrees volume is king for size and that overload should not be forced, but insists naturals still need to get stronger and move heavier weights (within a challenging intensity window) to keep tonnage rising, and warns that telling beginners they can grow from light 'fluff and puff' work invites laziness.

claims.claim: He asks permission before naming another YouTuber in a response video; small channels that name-drop for views without permission are pathetic, even if YouTube allows it.
Training experience leads to strength, and even genetic freaks who start very strong still get stronger as they train.
Bigger muscles produce more force, but it varies by individual: he has 20-inch legs and can barely squat 400 lbs, while some with 22-inch legs squat 500 lbs.
Gaining 100 lbs of mostly fat raises absolute strength (mass moves mass) but not pound-for-pound strength; you got heavier, not really stronger.
Excess bulk can change form so much on lifts like the deadlift that very big guys with large guts can barely get into position.
A big natural should be relatively strong and relatively old with many years of training; leverages and training history modify this.
A 19-year-old who is huge after claiming two years of training is on PEDs; even genetically gifted people need time to get big.
Progressive overload is both a result and a cause of growth (snake biting its tail): getting bigger lets you lift more, and lifting more makes you bigger.

You don't force progressive overload; it happens. Novice programs that add an arbitrary amount of plates every week until you stall are simplistic, lazy, and lead to injury, plateaus and people quitting before becoming intermediates.
There are multiple ways to overload a muscle; adding weight to the bar is the easiest to track but easier is not always better.

Athletes who hammer certain muscles (e.g. swimmers' lats) get huge development there, supporting volume as a hypertrophy driver, but bodybuilders can't replicate an elite athlete's regimen without neglecting the rest of the body.
You can borrow from sports training without doing the sport: he copies arm wrestlers' training for arm size without being an arm wrestler.
Muscle protein synthesis peaks around 60-75% of 1RM; there is no known hypertrophy benefit to RPE 10 singles.
It is better to squat 300 lbs for 5 than 350 lbs for 1 because total tonnage moved over the workout is far higher.

Find an intensity you can repeat safely with as much challenge as possible; if you can work at 80% of 1RM repeatedly, it boosts tonnage and growth even if it doesn't maximise protein synthesis per se.
Staying in a low-intensity rep range makes progress hard; include movements at higher intensity to drive strength up, not to show off, so that volume and tonnage can rise over the years.

You can maintain strength while losing size: in grad school, working 60 h/week, he only worked up to a 1RM bench and overhead press in 25-30 minutes, kept a three-plate bench for months with zero volume but lost lots of size.
The reverse also holds: away in the mountains with no gym and unable to squat, his legs barely shrank but he lost a lot of strength.
He has no experience with blood flow restriction training so won't comment; might try it someday if he can't reach 20-inch arms otherwise.

Strength is neural but not always trainable to the same degree: some people plateau fast neurally, and some untrained people with great leverages can outlift you on day one; strength is sometimes innate, and gifted people also improve faster and longer.
Volume matters much more than intensity for hypertrophy, but intensity should stay above roughly 40% 1RM because overall tonnage matters more than raw rep volume.
Equating tonnage at 40% vs 75% 1RM may give the same result in theory, but 40% takes much longer to complete; what matters is how much volume and intensity your body can recover from.
In his view the body responds to heavier weights rather than light 'fluff and puff'; low intensity drives less progress.
For naturals, heavy lifts like squats and deadlifts are believed to raise testosterone and GH, which matters to keep natural hormone production high.
Very high reps (40-50) are boring for most lifts; he only does those for neck and calves. Training needs to be fun.
Olympic lifters' relatively small legs don't prove strength doesn't equal size: they back squat infrequently, mostly as an accessory in off-season blocks, so their total squat volume is low.
20-rep squats grow the legs like nothing else; for leg hypertrophy volume is king.
Top Olympic lifters are genetic freaks with leverages you can't replicate; a muscle doesn't need to be as big if leverage is good. Stronger isn't necessarily bigger, but bigger is stronger.
Steroids don't just enhance natural potential; they create new potential. Poor natural producers who respond well to hormones are transformed, while good producers who respond poorly change little.
He speculates that a naive user taking low-dose PEDs could suppress natural levels that were higher than the exogenous dose.
Older people respond better to volume training than high intensity, which supports volume as a hypertrophy driver.
Drop sets are still progressive overload: a 225 lbs bench followed by a 195 lbs drop can be harder and create more stimulus than two sets of 225.
The Milo of Croton calf legend wouldn't work in reality (you can't control the calf's growth or recovery), and it actually illustrates growth through progressive overload.
Telling beginners they can get big from low intensity is dangerous because most people take the easy path and will pick non-challenging weights; you need to experience high intensity.
Using an enhanced pro like Dexter Jackson as an example for naturals is flawed: PEDs create growth from non-challenging weights, so naturals must be told they need to get stronger one way or another.
Moderate-weight workouts mean less injury risk, more frequency and higher weekly volume, which he agrees with, as long as you push close to maximal recoverable volume.

Many people doing 'volume' never really challenge themselves; being sore from 20 reps isn't enough. If you do sets of 12 back squats, in two years you must be moving much more weight or using less rest or harder tempo.

exercises.name: Back squat (20-rep sets)
exercises.why: high-rep squats grow legs like nothing else

exercises.name: Drop set bench press
exercises.why: working a fatigued muscle with lighter weight is still overload and may give more stimulus
